description:
Hi! I’m Hongyi Mei, an Astronomy student at the University of Toronto. I’m interested in exoplanets, AI for science, and making space science accessible.  More about me

I love Unity game development and I'm a strategy game enthusiast who loves the possibilities of learning through games!  I’m bringing these interests together in AstroCivilization, a game where children build space outposts and explore scientific decisions through play.
summary:
Artemis 2 is bringing human civilization back to Moon, would you help explore our civilization's future on Moon and Mars?

AstroCivilization puts children aged 7–12 in command of a lunar or Martian outpost. You will build a home, grow food, balance power and life support, and protect your crew during a solar storm. NASA data connects the challenge to real science, and adds in interesting facts to educate our children throughout the game. 

The game's story line features a fictional story of a kid in Mississauga, Ontario, and the path they gradually learn to become the commander of the outpost. 

Our goal is to take our game about balancing competing demands, to help the next generation see themselves as people who can handle the complicated tasks in the future of space exploration and in life. Childrens will learn about planning, trade-offs, and problem-solving, then connect those skills to their confidence about their future.
details:
Why I built AstroCiv

AstroCiv began with a game that made me want to explore the world beyond the game screen.

I used to be a student focused almost entirely on science, with little interest in the humanities. However, I discovered a strategy game in my first year of university, and that has sparked my interest in world history and humanities subjects. Leading the Inca empire across a virtual map made me curious about the actual civilization, and that curiosity eventually took me hiking in Peru.

I wanted to create that same spark for kids in the field of astronomy. My design philosophy is that children should enjoy playing enough to want to learn more. When knowledge helps them accomplish something they care about, they have a reason to seek it out. AstroCiv brings together my love of game development, astronomy, and learning through play.

How AstroCiv addresses the challenge

I chose to develop AstroCiv because it invites players to plan, weigh options, and anticipate consequences. In AstroCiv, you need to balance the limited resources to keep your missions successful.

For example, a greenhouse needs power, water and soil, which you need to first collect on lunar/martian surface. A solar storm forces players to protect their astronauts while postponing other goals. Players must balance these competing demands before time runs out. These decisions address the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge's main purpose, by encouraging kids to think and act quickly in the complexity of space missions.

NASA open data gives those game decisions a connection to real life science and scenarios. LRO/LOLA illumination informs lunar solar power, MOLA elevation data shapes Martian terrain, historical DONKI events inform the storm scenario, and OSDR findings connect the greenhouse to real research. Friendly pixel art and an unfolding story welcome young players into this science. Guided missions introduce one system at a time, while Free Build gives them room to experiment, make mistakes, and try again on different lunar/martian maps.


Working with NASA’s open data showed me how much science is freely available to anyone curious enough to look. I want to put that possibility within a child’s reach. A player who has guided a lunar crew through a storm has a reason to learn more about real science missions, and wonder how real astronauts would respond.

What is the intended impact?

My intended impact is to help children understand real mission trade-offs and inspire curiosity that continues after the game ends. I hope they leave seeking to learn more about science like solar flares, illumination on moon/mars, the effects of radiation on the human body. I also hope they can image themselves taking part in space exploration. A strategy game helped spark my curiosity about ancient civilizations and lead to a real Peru journey. AstroCiv is my attempt to offer another child a beginning of their own journey.

For children in Ontario, I hope the journey from a familiar hometown to a space outpost makes a future in science feel imaginable. For families, libraries and classrooms, the browser game could become a starting point for conversations about energy, food, resilience and teamwork.

I want to keep developing AstroCiv with children and educators: observe where beginners get stuck, improve readability and accessibility, and develop classroom activities that connect each mission to its science sources. Later missions could explore more resource and environmental tradeoffs.

AstroCiv is built with Unity, C#, offline NASA/CSA reference files and a WebGL browser build. Source code, data provenance, asset credits and AI-use disclosures accompany the project. NASA and CSA do not endorse AstroCiv, and its story and astronaut journey are fictional.
